articles.title: Health Wrap Episode 60 discusses healthcare spending, antimicrobial resistance and more
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The episode discuss trends in healthcare expenditure in India, concerns over the regulation of fertility services, the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance, and the impact of environmental and social conditions on public health

The 60th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu looks at key developments in public including healthcare financing, reproductive health, antimicrobial resistance, tuberculosis, environmental exposures and diabetes care.

Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss the latest National Health Accounts estimates for 2023–24, which show a substantial increase in government health expenditure and a decline in the share of household out-of-pocket spending nationally. The episode also examines the contrasting trends in Keralam, where household healthcare expenditure has increased and the share of government spending has declined.

The episode looks at the drug regulator’s direction to pharmaceutical companies to comply with revised prices for 137 anti-cancer drugs and the potential implications for treatment costs. It also examines concerns over an illegal human egg collection racket in Telangana, including questions about informed consent, women’s safety and the regulation of assisted reproductive technology centres. Developments in Karnataka’s proposed mid-life women’s health programme and mandatory gynaecological check-ups for girls are also discussed.

Marking World AMR Awareness Week, the episode explores the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance and the need for appropriate antibiotic use, timely diagnosis, infection prevention and surveillance. It also discusses phage therapy, which uses bacteriophages to target bacterial infections, and its potential role in addressing infections that do not respond to conventional antibiotics.

The discussion also examines tuberculosis through the lens of social and economic vulnerability, highlighting the importance of nutrition, housing and social support alongside diagnosis and treatment. It looks at the latest figures on domestic funding for India’s TB response, which now accounts for 86% of total spending, even as external funding declines.

The discussion also examines the health risks of extreme heat for pregnant women and newborns. A survey of healthcare professionals across five countries found that 98% of Indian clinicians surveyed had treated pregnant women and newborns whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat.

The episode also looks into how fear of diagnosis may discourage people from screening and discusses a Chennai initiative that uses dietary counselling by staff nurses to improve blood sugar control and support long-term diabetes management.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

The episode discuss trends in healthcare expenditure in India, concerns over the regulation of fertility services, the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance, and the impact of environmental and social conditions on public health

The 60th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu looks at key developments in public including healthcare financing, reproductive health, antimicrobial resistance, tuberculosis, environmental exposures and diabetes care.

Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss the latest National Health Accounts estimates for 2023–24, which show a substantial increase in government health expenditure and a decline in the share of household out-of-pocket spending nationally. The episode also examines the contrasting trends in Keralam, where household healthcare expenditure has increased and the share of government spending has declined.

The episode looks at the drug regulator’s direction to pharmaceutical companies to comply with revised prices for 137 anti-cancer drugs and the potential implications for treatment costs. It also examines concerns over an illegal human egg collection racket in Telangana, including questions about informed consent, women’s safety and the regulation of assisted reproductive technology centres. Developments in Karnataka’s proposed mid-life women’s health programme and mandatory gynaecological check-ups for girls are also discussed.

Marking World AMR Awareness Week, the episode explores the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance and the need for appropriate antibiotic use, timely diagnosis, infection prevention and surveillance. It also discusses phage therapy, which uses bacteriophages to target bacterial infections, and its potential role in addressing infections that do not respond to conventional antibiotics.

The discussion also examines tuberculosis through the lens of social and economic vulnerability, highlighting the importance of nutrition, housing and social support alongside diagnosis and treatment. It looks at the latest figures on domestic funding for India’s TB response, which now accounts for 86% of total spending, even as external funding declines.

The discussion also examines the health risks of extreme heat for pregnant women and newborns. A survey of healthcare professionals across five countries found that 98% of Indian clinicians surveyed had treated pregnant women and newborns whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat.

The episode also looks into how fear of diagnosis may discourage people from screening and discusses a Chennai initiative that uses dietary counselling by staff nurses to improve blood sugar control and support long-term diabetes management.

articles.title: One country, hundreds of dal recipes: exploring India’s diverse lentil traditions
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A look at how the humble ingredient travels through different soils, histories, cultures, climates, and kitchens

From Rajasthan in the west to Arunachal Pradesh in the east, from Kashmir in the north to Tamil Nadu in the south, India does dal in thousands of ways. There are no fixed proportions to what comes to the table, and everyone’s mother’s recipe is just right. From mamidikaya pappu , or mango dal , to palak dal and dal makhani , there is great diversity in how lentils are prepared across the country. Dal’s resonance here goes beyond the fact that India is the world’s largest producer and consumer of pulses: it is often a reminder of home, a longing for the simple things in life, and a connector of cultures.

That intimacy with dal , however, does not mean everyone makes it the same way — or even that home is where it tastes best. For Harpreet Singh, 26, the dal he cooks at the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) is far better than what is cooked at home. “It’s the ghee that makes the difference,” he says with a laugh, adding that at home, it is rationed. At the temple, five kilos of ghee are added to a quintal of dal . “But the real secret is that we add sarson ka tel [mustard oil] once the dal is boiled, after the mail [froth] on top has been skimmed off,” he says.

Singh’s companion cook adds that it is also the pre-dawn prayers that go into the degchis (wide-mouthed cooking pots) , some of which can hold up to four quintals of dal , which also takes 100 kg of onion, 24 kg of salt, 16 kg of ginger and garlic each, 6 kg of turmeric powder, and 5 kg of khada masala (whole spices). The gurbani (reading of the scriptures) plays on a loudspeaker through the kitchens and service area.

Amritsar’s Golden Temple feeds 70,000 to 80,000 people on weekdays, with the number going to over a lakh on special weekends like amavasya (new moon), and up to 2.5 lakh on a guru’s birthday. In the kitchen, three shifts of about 450 people cook 15-20 quintals of dal daily, over wood-fired stoves. The most popular dal dish here is the mixed variety, which is boiled for six hours. In the langar , a free communal dining hall spread across several rooms and capable of seating 3,000 people at a time, dal is a staple. “Everyone is happy eating it,” says Singh, adding that people also pack food in vessels for patients in hospitals.

From former India cricket captain Harmanpreet Kaur’s fondness for dal and rice while playing for India, to Lok Sabha MP Mahua Moitra bringing her home-cooked dal and bhindi to Parliament, and the slow-cooked, indulgent Dal Raisina served at Rashtrapati Bhavan, dal cuts across social and culinary divides. It is one of India’s most unassuming yet enduring staples — everyday comfort food that can be as humble or elaborate as the occasion demands.

articles.title: Three cyclones in three weeks: What’s happening in the Bay of Bengal? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Such a frequency is uncommon but not unique this year; there were around 1.8 cyclones a year in the post-monsoon period in 1982-2022, with the average increasing after 2001

The story so far: Within 23 days this year, three cyclones formed over the Bay of Bengal. Of them, Cyclone Arnab made landfall near Yanam on the Andhra Pradesh coast on October 28 and Murasu on November 3 near Ongole. Cyclone Akvan formed on November 16 and made landfall near Gopalpur in Odisha on Friday morning (November 20, 2026).

A cyclone requires an atmospheric disturbance, abundant moisture, and favourable winds. The Bay has two main cyclone seasons, April-May and October-December. During the southwest monsoon, strong winds blowing in different directions at different altitudes suppress cyclone formation. But as the monsoon withdraws, the vertical wind shear weakens even as the waters remain warm, creating more favourable conditions.

articles.title: Andhra Pradesh gets national recognition for its progress in HIV/AIDS control
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Six districts in the State have achieved ‘Surakshit’ status and another 10 the ‘Saksham’ status, and the rankings are based on a district’s performance on 95-95-95 targets fixed by the Joint United Nations Programme
Andhra Pradesh has received national recognition for its progress in controlling HIV, with six districts in the State achieving the ‘Surakshit’ status and another 10 achieving the ‘Saksham’ status.

According to a release from the department, the districts of Chittoor, East Godavari, Guntur, Kakinada, Visakhapatnam and Vizianagaram achieved ‘Surakshit’ status, while the districts of Anakapalli, Anantapur, Bapatla, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, Eluru, Kurnool, Parvathipuram-Manyam, Srikakulam, Tirupati and YSR Kadapa achieved the ‘Saksham’ status.
The rankings are based on a district’s performance on 95-95-95 targets, fixed by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS(UNAIDS) as part of efforts to end the epidemic by 2030.

The three targets include ensuring that 95% of people living with HIV know their status, providing antiretroviral therapy (ART) to 95% of those diagnosed; and achieving viral suppression in 95% of those receiving treatment.

According to the release, the percentage of people living with HIV who knew their status increased from 87.7% in April 2026 to 92.7% in October, and currently stands at 92.8%. Between April and October, 7,641 new HIV cases were identified through Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres.
The number of people receiving ART increased from 2,41,507 in April to 2,65,690 in October, an additional 24,183 patients. Viral suppression has been achieved in 96.4% of those undergoing treatment.
Reacting to the development, Minister for Health, Medical and Family Welfare Satya Kumar Yadav said 16 districts improved their performance between April and October.

The release stated that the A.P. State AIDS Control Society (APSACS) developed ‘Suraksha’ portal to monitor HIV testing, diagnosis and treatment services. It also launched ‘Each One Reach One’ initiative, to bring patients who had discontinued medication back into treatment. These two measures also helped the State achieve the targets.
Mr. Satya Kumar said priority was to ensure timely diagnosis, continuous treatment and quality healthcare without discrimination for everyone living with HIV.
APSACS Project Director Smaran Raj said the organisation was committed to bringing three more districts to ‘Surakshit’ status in the week.

articles.title: Healthcare AI: hospitals lack capacity to measure real-world patient outcomes, warns French expert
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Emmanuel Bacry warns that laboratory accuracy scores do not establish real-world clinical benefits; says healthcare AI trained largely on Western data may not work elsewhere

Hospitals worldwide are ill-equipped to assess whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems deployed in their facilities actually improve patient outcomes, raising questions about the clinical and economic value of healthcare AI, Emmanuel Bacry, Scientific Director of France’s Health Data Hub, said at the Bengaluru Tech Summit.

“There are maybe six or seven hospitals in the whole world today that are able to evaluate medical devices deployed in their system,” Mr. Bacry said. Hospitals struggle to access and integrate patient information to track outcomes after discharge, including recovery rates and mortality, making it difficult to establish the actual impact of AI-based medical technologies.
“In hospitals, we don’t know how to compute that,” he said, referring to the return on investment of such technologies. “So imagine now, if they adopt AI.”

Mr. Bacry cited an alert system based on rules-based AI, or an expert system, designed to warn intensive care unit (ICU) staff about severe kidney failure. Despite functioning effectively, the system was associated with a doubling of deaths in two of the six US hospitals where it was deployed in 2022, he said. He did not identify the study.

articles.title: Congress hopeful of U.P. alliance with SP, seeks ‘respectable’ seat-sharing
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: ‘We were weak, but we are not weak now. We have the best leader in this country right now, as only we can handle the BJP better than any other party,’ says Rajendra Pal Gautam

The Congress is hopeful of forging an alliance with the Samajwadi Party (SP) for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election but wants a “respectable” seat-sharing arrangement, All India Congress Committee in-charge for the State Rajendra Pal Gautam has said.

Mr. Gautam, in an interview with The Hindu , said the two parties are expected to hold formal seat-sharing discussions this week and asserted that the Congress would make the alleged “ chanda chori ” (theft of temple donations) a major campaign issue.

Though he did not disclose the exact date, the first meeting is likely to be held on Monday afternoon. Senior leaders, including Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, K.C. Venugopal, and Mr. Gautam, are expected to participate.

Commenting on SP chief Akhilesh Yadav’s recent statement that the Congress had sought 181 seats, Mr. Gautam said, “I am not going to reveal which seats, but we have given them a list. We will try to convince them, and I am sure they will try to convince us. The outcome depends on these talks.”
Asked whether the Congress would settle for an alliance at any cost, Mr. Gautam said: “It is not like that at all. The understanding will be a respectable one.”

Countering suggestions that the Congress lacked the organisational strength to bargain for a substantial share of seats, Mr. Gautam pointed out that while the SP won 37 seats and the Congress six in the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the SP’s alliance with the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) in the 2019 Lok Sabha polls had not yielded similar results.
“We were weak, but we are not weak now,” he said, adding, “We have the best leader in this country right now, as only we can handle the BJP better than any other party.”

On whether the Congress was attempting social engineering to regain the support of the Brahmin, Dalit, and Muslim communities that had once formed its core constituency, he claimed that every section of society is now gravitating toward the party. “Every section is feeling cheated, whether Brahmins, Dalits, OBCs, or Muslims,” he said.

The party also intends to highlight the alleged chadhava-chori (theft of offerings and donations) at Lord Ram’s temple in Ayodhya. The campaign, scheduled to begin in the first week of December, will take the issue to villages, chaupals, and gram panchayats.

“ Chadhava-chori, chanda-chori will be one of our main issues in the election. The BJP came to power using faith and then betrayed the people. In every press conference and public meeting, we will raise it,” he said.

articles.title: Plan approach paper eyes leveraging heft of Keralam’s economy for 15th Five-Year Plan period
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The UDF government and the Planning Board have visualised a ‘partnership economy’ for building the economy up from ₹16 lakh crore to ₹28 lakh crore by 2031-32

In targeting a 7% growth in real terms during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2027-2032), the UDF government is hoping to leverage the heft of Keralam’s economy, which, according to the State Planning Board’s approach paper to the 15th Plan, “contains far more capital than its government commands.”

Real growth of 7% a year for five years (2027-2032) at the incremental capital-output ratio (the measure of how much investment is needed to generate a unit of economic growth) of around 4, implies investment of ₹4.5 lakh crore a year, according to the approach paper. The 2026-27 Revised Budget on the other hand estimates a capital expenditure of only ₹22,566 crore. “About ₹19 in ₹20 of the investment Keralam needs will therefore come from outside the State Budget,” the paper, published last week, notes.

On money outside the Budget, the approach paper has this to say: “Bank deposits stand at ₹10,84,241 crore and advances at ₹7,81,043 crore, a credit-deposit ratio of 72.04%. Non-resident deposits are ₹2,86,063 crore. Primary agricultural credit societies hold nearly ₹1.3 lakh crore, about 70% of all such deposits in the country. Remittances were ₹2,16,893 crore in 2023. Bank lending depends on the availability of bankable projects, so the gap between deposits and advances measures the shortage of bankable projects in the State more than any shortage of savings. If credit to the Plan’s engines rose by the equivalent of 8% points of deposits, about ₹87,000 crore more would be at work in Keralam, nearly four times the annual capital budget.”
The task of planning will therefore be to direct that capital to productive use within the State, according to the paper.
The UDF government and the Planning Board have visualised a ‘partnership economy’ for building the economy up from ₹16 lakh crore to ₹28 lakh crore by 2031-32.

The approach paper to the 14th Five-Year Plan had noted that mobilising resources for the Plan period (2022-2027) would be a “challenging task.” The scenario has not changed much. The White Paper on Keralam’s fiscal health laid in the Legislative Assembly in June this year had observed that “behind Keralam’s social achievements lies a fiscal structure that is under serious and growing strain.”

The approach paper for the 15th Plan draws a grim picture of present-day Keralam. The State is a “picture of slow growth, low investment, large youth unemployment and an ageing population. The State’s fiscal space is rather limited, and its revenue base is weak. There is no hope of large Union transfers.”

🏛️ Political, National & Polity 📅 22 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 3 Min Read

📰 Plan approach paper eyes leveraging heft of Keralam’s economy for 15th Five-Year Plan period

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

The UDF government and the Planning Board have visualised a ‘partnership economy’ for building the economy up from ₹16 lakh crore to ₹28 lakh crore by 2031-32

In targeting a 7% growth in real terms during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2027-2032), the UDF government is hoping to leverage the heft of Keralam’s economy, which, according to the State Planning Board’s approach paper to the 15th Plan, “contains far more capital than its government commands.”

Real growth of 7% a year for five years (2027-2032) at the incremental capital-output ratio (the measure of how much investment is needed to generate a unit of economic growth) of around 4, implies investment of ₹4.5 lakh crore a year, according to the approach paper. The 2026-27 Revised Budget on the other hand estimates a capital expenditure of only ₹22,566 crore. “About ₹19 in ₹20 of the investment Keralam needs will therefore come from outside the State Budget,” the paper, published last week, notes.

On money outside the Budget, the approach paper has this to say: “Bank deposits stand at ₹10,84,241 crore and advances at ₹7,81,043 crore, a credit-deposit ratio of 72.04%. Non-resident deposits are ₹2,86,063 crore. Primary agricultural credit societies hold nearly ₹1.3 lakh crore, about 70% of all such deposits in the country. Remittances were ₹2,16,893 crore in 2023. Bank lending depends on the availability of bankable projects, so the gap between deposits and advances measures the shortage of bankable projects in the State more than any shortage of savings. If credit to the Plan’s engines rose by the equivalent of 8% points of deposits, about ₹87,000 crore more would be at work in Keralam, nearly four times the annual capital budget.”

The task of planning will therefore be to direct that capital to productive use within the State, according to the paper.

The UDF government and the Planning Board have visualised a ‘partnership economy’ for building the economy up from ₹16 lakh crore to ₹28 lakh crore by 2031-32.

The approach paper to the 14th Five-Year Plan had noted that mobilising resources for the Plan period (2022-2027) would be a “challenging task.” The scenario has not changed much. The White Paper on Keralam’s fiscal health laid in the Legislative Assembly in June this year had observed that “behind Keralam’s social achievements lies a fiscal structure that is under serious and growing strain.”

The approach paper for the 15th Plan draws a grim picture of present-day Keralam. The State is a “picture of slow growth, low investment, large youth unemployment and an ageing population. The State’s fiscal space is rather limited, and its revenue base is weak. There is no hope of large Union transfers.”

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: The approach paper for the 15th Plan draws a grim picture of present-day Keralam. The State is a “picture of slow growth, low investment, large youth unemployment and an ageing population. The State’s fiscal space is rather limited, and its revenue base is weak. There is no hope of large Union transfers.”

articles.title: CJP plans to take ‘Cockroach Club’ across India, shifts youth movement beyond street protests
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Launched in Pune with over 300 participants, the initiative will combine political debates, lectures, film screenings, comedy and cultural performances as the party seeks to channelise youth energy into shaping India’s future

Moving beyond street mobilisation, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is looking to build a nationwide network of cultural and discussion spaces with its newly launched ‘Cockroach Club’. The party wants the initiative to reach every part of the country, including remote villages, as it seeks to give young people a platform to debate public issues, exchange ideas and envision the future they want for India, its co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka said during an interaction with The Hindu.

The club’s first gathering, titled ‘Legacy of Bapu’, was held in Pune on November 21 and brought together more than 300 people for an event lasting around three hours. The programme featured comedy, satire and conversations on Mahatma Gandhi, while participants discussed local issues concerning Maharashtra. Performances addressing larger issues facing the country were also part of the event.

“This is a platform where we can all come together and articulate the future we want for ourselves and answer some difficult questions we want to address. The idea of Cockroach Clubs is to have a space where people can come, talk, brainstorm, collaborate and envision what they want our country to be,” Mr. Ranka said.

Explaining why Pune was chosen for the first gathering, he said the party had a large support base in Maharashtra, while Delhi was also an important centre for the organisation and would soon feature in its plans.
“The idea is for the Cockroach Club to go to every corner of the country. This is a truly national movement and everything has to come together,” he added.

CJP co-convenor Saurav Das said the club was envisioned as a “physical space for the younger generation” to come together, exchange ideas, question, learn and grow. It would host lectures and discussions on the ideas of Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, B.R. Ambedkar and other thinkers, besides film screenings, live performances and stand-up comedy.
The space would also offer young people a quiet corner to read, study, and prepare for examinations, while allowing them to unwind and interact, he said.

“This was just a trailer. As we go ahead, we will know what can be bettered. We will use this platform to discuss how to take this movement forward, how to get more and more people to join, and channelise the energy of the youth in a structured manner to bring a change in the country,” Mr. Das said.

He said the club would encourage young people to think for themselves rather than have opinions handed down to them or ideologies imposed on them. “We the young will develop our Idea of India at the Cockroach Club,” he said.
Over 300 people gathered at the Gandhi Bhavan, Kothrud in Pune for Cockroach Club’s first gathering, titled ‘Legacy of Bapu’, was held in Pune on November 21. Photo credit: Special Arrangement.

articles.title: NHAI yet to act despite 300 complaints of inordinate delay at Chowlagere toll plaza on NH 75 Hassan-Sakleshpur section
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Authority says it will raise the issue with Indian Highways Management Company that handles FASTag of vehicles

Road users have alleged frequent delays in clearing of the vehicles, particularly those with annual FASTag at the Chowlagere Toll Plaza on Bengaluru-Mangaluru National Highway 75 between Hassan and Sakleshpur and rude behaviour by the personnel manning the facility.

Chowlagere toll plaza near Alur in Hassan district is a part of NH 75 four-lane project between Hassan and Maranahalli (about 45 km) executed by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI). The four-lane work got completed a couple of years ago with much delay.

Annoyed with the frequent delays faced by him personally, P. Aditya Narayan from Puttur, a regular traveller on the section sought details of similar complaints under the Right to Information Act from the NHAI. For his surprise, a November 20 reply from the Authority informed that as many as 300 complaints were made to the NHAI, 205 through the Rajmarg Yatra Portal and 95 through 1033 NHAI Helpline between April and November 15, 2026.

During the period, three complaints were received about the staff misbehaviour with road users, the Authority said in the reply. Majority of the causes for the delay in lifting of the toll barrier included software problem, connection failure and a few issues of hardware failure, the reply said.

Mr. Narayan said the scanner often took an unusually long time to read the FASTag. “We were forced to wait, honk twice or thrice and eventually the toll staff contact the control room over walkie-talkie, communicate the vehicle number and get the passage cleared manually.”

After he brought the issue to MLC Kishore Kumar’s notice, the legislator wrote to the NHAI to immediately address the issue. Still, the Authority has not rectified the mistake in the system, he regretted.

Janekere Paramesh, a photojournalist from Sakleshpur who often travels to Hassan, endorses the complaints and said ever since the Chowlagere toll plaza was commissioned, road users have been facing problems of delayed clearance. Rude behaviour by the plaza personnel adds to the agony of road users, he said adding en-number of complaints to the Authority have remained unaddressed.
Mr. Narayan further said FASTag annual pass-holders face similar delays in many other toll plazas across the State.

Stating that the NHAI does not directly handle FASTag issues, as it is being dealt with by Indian Highways Management Company Ltd., the Authority’s Karnataka Regional Officer V. P. Brahmankar told The Hindu that he would raise the issue with its CEO regarding the System Integrator or changing the Integrator. “I will ask the CEO to verify the system and take necessary steps to update it,” he said.

NHAI Hassan Project Implementation Unit (PIU) Director K. Mathivanan told The Hindu that the Chowlagere Plaza was among the many where the Authority used a new construction design to save on space and buildings. There were some ‘frequency’ issues [between the FASTag and the reader] because of the narrow toll lanes. “We will resolve the issue by immediately taking it up with the IHMCL,” he said.

The Authority says it will raise the issue with Indian Highways Management Company that handles FASTag of vehicles

Road users have alleged frequent delays in clearing of the vehicles, particularly those with annual FASTag at the Chowlagere Toll Plaza on Bengaluru-Mangaluru National Highway 75 between Hassan and Sakleshpur and rude behaviour by the personnel manning the facility.

Chowlagere toll plaza near Alur in Hassan district is a part of NH 75 four-lane project between Hassan and Maranahalli (about 45 km) executed by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI). The four-lane work got completed a couple of years ago with much delay.

Annoyed with the frequent delays faced by him personally, P. Aditya Narayan from Puttur, a regular traveller on the section sought details of similar complaints under the Right to Information Act from the NHAI. For his surprise, a November 20 reply from the Authority informed that as many as 300 complaints were made to the NHAI, 205 through the Rajmarg Yatra Portal and 95 through 1033 NHAI Helpline between April and November 15, 2026.

During the period, three complaints were received about the staff misbehaviour with road users, the Authority said in the reply. Majority of the causes for the delay in lifting of the toll barrier included software problem, connection failure and a few issues of hardware failure, the reply said.

Mr. Narayan said the scanner often took an unusually long time to read the FASTag. “We were forced to wait, honk twice or thrice and eventually the toll staff contact the control room over walkie-talkie, communicate the vehicle number and get the passage cleared manually.”

After he brought the issue to MLC Kishore Kumar’s notice, the legislator wrote to the NHAI to immediately address the issue. Still, the Authority has not rectified the mistake in the system, he regretted.

Janekere Paramesh, a photojournalist from Sakleshpur who often travels to Hassan, endorses the complaints and said ever since the Chowlagere toll plaza was commissioned, road users have been facing problems of delayed clearance. Rude behaviour by the plaza personnel adds to the agony of road users, he said adding en-number of complaints to the Authority have remained unaddressed.

Mr. Narayan further said FASTag annual pass-holders face similar delays in many other toll plazas across the State.

Stating that the NHAI does not directly handle FASTag issues, as it is being dealt with by Indian Highways Management Company Ltd., the Authority’s Karnataka Regional Officer V. P. Brahmankar told The Hindu that he would raise the issue with its CEO regarding the System Integrator or changing the Integrator. “I will ask the CEO to verify the system and take necessary steps to update it,” he said.

NHAI Hassan Project Implementation Unit (PIU) Director K. Mathivanan told The Hindu that the Chowlagere Plaza was among the many where the Authority used a new construction design to save on space and buildings. There were some ‘frequency’ issues [between the FASTag and the reader] because of the narrow toll lanes. “We will resolve the issue by immediately taking it up with the IHMCL,” he said.

articles.title: JKSSB exam cheating racket: Six more arrested; six government employees among accused
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Police said the question paper was allegedly taken out of the examination centre, photographed and circulated among selected candidates through Telegram

Six more persons were arrested in the ongoing investigation into the Finance Accounts Assistant (FAA) examination conducted recently by Jammu & Kashmir Services Selection Board, taking the total arrests to 20, with police clarifying that the malpractice was confined to a specific examination centre and did not involve a paper leak.

The accused include six government employees, among them the alleged mastermind. Police said the question paper was allegedly taken out of the examination centre, photographed and circulated among selected candidates through Telegram.
14 arrested as J&K Police bust exam cheating racket; mobiles, wireless sets seized

The investigation has also revealed financial transactions of ₹1.80 lakh, of which ₹1.40 lakh has been recovered, while the accused had allegedly negotiated payments of ₹10–12 lakh from candidates in exchange for helping them clear the examination, Jammu Senior Superintendent of Police Joginder Singh said at a press conference in Jammu.

On November 15, police in Jammu arrested 14 suspects ahead of the FAA exam, “uncovering” a network that planned to transmit answers to select candidates inside the exam centres through electronic communication devices.
Several wireless radio sets were seized in the intelligence-based operation, three FIRs were lodged, and a Special Investigation Team (SIT) was constituted to probe the alleged conspiracy.

Disclosing details of the investigation, the SSP said the probe had led to the identification and arrest of the alleged main kingpin, whose interrogation brought to light a wider network involving candidates, government employees and other intermediaries.

"Of the 20 persons arrested so far, six are government employees. Their details have been shared with the respective departments for departmental action. At the same time, criminal proceedings are also being pursued based on their alleged roles," he said, clarifying that none of the arrested persons belonged to the JKSSB.
According to the investigation, Mr. Singh said the alleged mastermind had initially planned to facilitate cheating for two persons — a close relative and a friend.

However, another accused involved in the operation allegedly created a separate network and contacted 20 to 22 additional candidates. He reportedly collected their original documents and obtained blank cheques from four to five candidates, with an understanding that payments would be made after they successfully cleared the examination.

articles.title: SCO Civilisational Dialogue ‘leaves options open’ for Pakistan SCO meets next year, say sources
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: As the government faces criticism over “inconsistency” in the invitation to Pakistan, officials say the invite can be seen as building a window of opportunity for “common civility”

The visit of Pakistan Minister for Environment and Climate Change, Musadik Malik, to India, the first by any senior Pakistani official since 2023, was a “Shanghai Cooperation Organisation” (SCO) initiative, not an Indian one alone, said officials as the government came under criticism from the Opposition.

However, former Indian diplomats who served in Pakistan said the visit and the invitation to the SCO Civilisational Dialogue in Delhi and the SCO Summit to be held in Pakistan next year could be seen as building a window of opportunity for “common civility” and providing a multilateral platform for the region, when bilateral moves, and the SAARC Summit are not taking place.

Ministry of External Affairs officials have stressed that there were no “bilateral” or one-to-one meetings during the three-day event hosted at Delhi’s iconic Purana Kila (Old Fort) monument. Ministers from six countries – Pakistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Azerbaijan, Iran, and the Kyrgyz Republic – and Deputy Ministers from eight other countries participated in the forum.

Government officials pointed out that the event allows India a chance to highlight its cultural prowess and strong roots and furthers India’s common links with other members of the SCO, which also see themselves as “civilizational” states. It is also significant that India has carved out a space for itself in the year when Pakistan is the Chair of the SCO, they said, and is leading a shift in the grouping’s more security-oriented and land-locked focus to a more South Asian, oceanic and people-to-people linked focus.

They suggested that such meetings could also pave the way for next year, when External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will all be invited to Pakistan for SCO meetings chaired by Pakistan, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be invited to the Heads of Council meeting to be held in the third quarter of 2027. Government officials said it was too early to speak about participation in these meetings in Pakistan yet, but that a decision closer to the dates would only be possible if options were kept open at present, and SCO events in the run-up to the Summit are kept away from the “negativity” of bilateral relations.

“The meeting was in an SCO context so it would be inappropriate to read into it any bilateral content, leave alone a breakthrough,” said former Indian High Commissioner to Islamabad TCA Raghavan (2013-2015). He added, however, that “given the precarious and fraught state of India- Pakistan relations, an episode of common civility and normalcy is a plus and, even without intending to, creates possibilities.”

Former High Commissioner to Islamabad Ajay Bisaria (2017-2019), who was the last to serve in Pakistan before both sides downgraded ties in 2019, said that Mr. Malik’s visit to India represented “more than a formality but less than a thaw” and demonstrated how such multilateral events allow India and Pakistan to “tolerate each other’s presence, even when they won’t engage directly”. When asked about India’s attendance at SCO events in Pakistan next year, Mr. Bisaria said that the “ball is in Pakistan’s court” to “dial down both terrorism and rhetoric” if it hopes for Indian leaders to travel there. Significantly, he said such an event could be an opportunity to revive the SAARC process as well, that has been suspended for a decade.

On Friday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, making the point that while “empires had redrawn maps”, such dialogues had “transformed and enriched global thought”. Mr. Modi had proposed the Dialogue at the SCO Summit in Tianjin in 2025, and the proposal was adopted at the SCO Summit in Bishkek in October 2026, with the declaration announcing that it would be held in Delhi this month.

The criticism was particularly sharp over images this weekend of Mr. Modi and the Pakistani Minister seated in the first row, as well as of Culture Minister and host Gajendra Singh Shekhawat holding a conversation with Mr. Malik at a lunch table.

“This is a multilateral event within the SCO framework, for which invitations have been extended to all members of the SCO, including Pakistan,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, underlining at briefings held in the past week that the government has not changed its position on other outstanding bilateral issues with Pakistan including over the Pahalgam terror attack, and the suspension of the Indus Water Treaty.

🏛️ Political, National & Polity 📅 22 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 6 Min Read

📰 SCO Civilisational Dialogue ‘leaves options open’ for Pakistan SCO meets next year, say sources

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

As the government faces criticism over “inconsistency” in the invitation to Pakistan, officials say the invite can be seen as building a window of opportunity for “common civility”

The visit of Pakistan Minister for Environment and Climate Change, Musadik Malik, to India, the first by any senior Pakistani official since 2023, was a “Shanghai Cooperation Organisation” (SCO) initiative, not an Indian one alone, said officials as the government came under criticism from the Opposition.

However, former Indian diplomats who served in Pakistan said the visit and the invitation to the SCO Civilisational Dialogue in Delhi and the SCO Summit to be held in Pakistan next year could be seen as building a window of opportunity for “common civility” and providing a multilateral platform for the region, when bilateral moves, and the SAARC Summit are not taking place.

Ministry of External Affairs officials have stressed that there were no “bilateral” or one-to-one meetings during the three-day event hosted at Delhi’s iconic Purana Kila (Old Fort) monument. Ministers from six countries – Pakistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Azerbaijan, Iran, and the Kyrgyz Republic – and Deputy Ministers from eight other countries participated in the forum.

Government officials pointed out that the event allows India a chance to highlight its cultural prowess and strong roots and furthers India’s common links with other members of the SCO, which also see themselves as “civilizational” states. It is also significant that India has carved out a space for itself in the year when Pakistan is the Chair of the SCO, they said, and is leading a shift in the grouping’s more security-oriented and land-locked focus to a more South Asian, oceanic and people-to-people linked focus.

They suggested that such meetings could also pave the way for next year, when External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will all be invited to Pakistan for SCO meetings chaired by Pakistan, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be invited to the Heads of Council meeting to be held in the third quarter of 2027. Government officials said it was too early to speak about participation in these meetings in Pakistan yet, but that a decision closer to the dates would only be possible if options were kept open at present, and SCO events in the run-up to the Summit are kept away from the “negativity” of bilateral relations.

“The meeting was in an SCO context so it would be inappropriate to read into it any bilateral content, leave alone a breakthrough,” said former Indian High Commissioner to Islamabad TCA Raghavan (2013-2015). He added, however, that “given the precarious and fraught state of India- Pakistan relations, an episode of common civility and normalcy is a plus and, even without intending to, creates possibilities.”

Former High Commissioner to Islamabad Ajay Bisaria (2017-2019), who was the last to serve in Pakistan before both sides downgraded ties in 2019, said that Mr. Malik’s visit to India represented “more than a formality but less than a thaw” and demonstrated how such multilateral events allow India and Pakistan to “tolerate each other’s presence, even when they won’t engage directly”. When asked about India’s attendance at SCO events in Pakistan next year, Mr. Bisaria said that the “ball is in Pakistan’s court” to “dial down both terrorism and rhetoric” if it hopes for Indian leaders to travel there. Significantly, he said such an event could be an opportunity to revive the SAARC process as well, that has been suspended for a decade.

On Friday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, making the point that while “empires had redrawn maps”, such dialogues had “transformed and enriched global thought”. Mr. Modi had proposed the Dialogue at the SCO Summit in Tianjin in 2025, and the proposal was adopted at the SCO Summit in Bishkek in October 2026, with the declaration announcing that it would be held in Delhi this month.

The criticism was particularly sharp over images this weekend of Mr. Modi and the Pakistani Minister seated in the first row, as well as of Culture Minister and host Gajendra Singh Shekhawat holding a conversation with Mr. Malik at a lunch table.

“This is a multilateral event within the SCO framework, for which invitations have been extended to all members of the SCO, including Pakistan,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, underlining at briefings held in the past week that the government has not changed its position on other outstanding bilateral issues with Pakistan including over the Pahalgam terror attack, and the suspension of the Indus Water Treaty.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: “This is a multilateral event within the SCO framework, for which invitations have been extended to all members of the SCO, including Pakistan,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, underlining at briefings held in the past week that the government has not changed its position on other outstanding bilateral issues with Pakistan including over the Pahalgam terror attack, and the suspension of the Indus Water Treaty.

articles.title: Rebels kill 15 in South Sudan
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: An official hinted at fighters loyal to the country's former first Vice-President Riek Machar, a longtime rival of President Salva Kiir who has been under house arrest since March 2025
An attack on Sunday (November 22, 2026) by rebels in northwestern South Sudan has killed at least 15 civilians, with the toll likely to rise, local sources told AFP .
One official pointed the finger at fighters loyal to the country's former first Vice-President Riek Machar, a longtime rival of President Salva Kiir who has been under house arrest since March 2025.

“The attack on the Bol Bol Boma area in Tonj East County, Warrap State, began late on Saturday,” Machuei Bith, the county's caretaker commissioner, told AFP . He blamed the deaths on fighters from neighbouring Unity State belonging to Machar's SPLA-IO armed group.

"Fifteen civilians and cattle keepers were killed and four armed attackers with SPLA-IO uniforms were also killed," he told AFP . A local police officer confirmed the story on condition of anonymity and said the fighting was still ongoing on Sunday morning. "Further details on casualties from both sides will be shared later on with the media," the officer said.
23 dead in clashes between South Sudan government, opposition forces

Since independence from Sudan in 2011, the world's youngest country has been forced to grapple with various violent conflicts, linked to political infighting, ethnic tensions or competition for resources.
Between 2013 and 2018, the eastern African country was torn apart by a civil war pitting forces loyal to Machar against those supporting Kiir, which left more than 4,00,000 people dead.

articles.title: India-EU trade pact likely to be signed on December 16
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: European Union's Ambassador to India, Jean-Eric Paquet, recently said the FTA will be signed during PM Modi's visit to Brussels in December, and it will come into force in 2027

India and the 27-nation bloc European Union (EU) are likely to sign the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) on December 16, an official said. The two sides concluded the negotiations for the pact on January 27 this year.

European Union's Ambassador to India, Jean-Eric Paquet, recently said the FTA will be signed during Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi 's visit to Brussels in December, and it will come into force next year.

The European Commission has already submitted proposals to the Council of the European Union seeking authorisation for signing and conclusion of the agreement, along with the final legal text and tariff schedules.

Under the free trade agreement, described as 'mother of all deals', 93 per cent of Indian shipments will enjoy duty-free access to the 27-nation bloc, while imports of luxury cars and wines from the EU will become less expensive.

The deal, concluded after negotiations spanning over two decades, will create a market of about 2 billion people across the world's fourth-largest economy, India, and the second-largest economic bloc, the EU.
Watch | India–EU Free Trade Agreement explained: Biggest trade deal in India’s history | India-New Zealand FTA comes into force; new visa categories for Indians, zero-duty access for exports
Taken together, India and the EU account for 25% of global GDP and one-third (about USD 11 trillion) of international trade (about $33 trillion).
The EU is India's largest trading partner in goods among individual blocs, while India ranks as the EU's ninth-largest goods trading partner globally and sixth in services.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted Houthi missile in western region
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Saudi Arabia's western region contains key energy infrastructure including the Yanbu terminal, a major facility for crude oil exports
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said on Sunday (November 22, 2026) it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward the kingdom's western Red Sea coast.
"Air defence intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the western region," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a social media post.

Saudi Arabia's western region contains key energy infrastructure including the Yanbu terminal, a major facility for crude oil exports, and the Jazan refinery in the far southwest of the country bordering Yemen.
Houthi fighters have attacked these major oil installations in recent weeks, alongside strikes on airports and military sites.
Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government against the Houthis, is the world's largest crude exporter.
Houthi attacks have killed 26 people in Saudi Arabia since September, including 23 in strikes on airports, according to the kingdom's authorities.

On Thursday (November 19), a tower housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund in Riyadh's financial district sustained damage on several floors in a Houthi attack, authorities said.
A skyscraper belonging to state oil giant Aramco was also damaged in a strike at the beginning of the month.

articles.title: Giving India’s first practicing woman doctor her due: Kadambini Ganguly​
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Kadambini Ganguly broke barriers to become one of India’s first women physicians to practise Western medicine

As far as trailblazers go, Kadambini Ganguly will figure right on top of several lists. She was a pioneering woman physician, the first to practice successfully in India, a gynaecologist and a social reformer who, equally efficiently, managed a large family as well. The story of Kadambini Ganguly is one of extraordinary achievement, and if told widely, will continue to inspire the young women of today.

In a profile published in Cureus in 2024, the authors point to the influence of the progressive Bramho Samaj movement, initiated by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, that helped Kadambini emerge from the shackles of conservative orthodoxy that might have stiffled her immense talent. “This environment, which championed the values of education and gender equality, contributed significantly to shaping her exemplary career and lifelong dedication to social justice,” the article reads. Records of her life acknowledge that she was partly recognised during her lifetime, but also mercilessly criticised and defamed for being a progressive, working woman. The full recognition of her contributions in medicine and the social sector came much later, only in recent decades.

Science, Space & Environment Report: Giving India’s first practicing woman doctor her due: Kadambini Ganguly​. This milestone highlights indigenous research, technological self-reliance, and environmental sustainability.

fullParagraphs: Attappady’s recurring infant deaths this year point to a crisis that goes beyond malnutrition and access to timely healthcare. Poverty, land alienation, and the erosion of traditional food systems, are taking a toll on maternal and child health in this predominantly tribal region of Keralam

Between the pages of a logbook recording Dakshina’s treatment are ₹100, ₹50, ₹20, and ₹10 notes. Dakshina’s mother, Minnal Rani, had filed them away for her daughter’s medical expenses. The child is gone, but the money remains untouched. “We will never spend it,” she says, fighting back tears.

Dakshina was five months old when doctors detected a hole in her heart. Born on June 13, 2025, she was taken to many hospitals, including one in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam’s capital. With surgery ruled out, she was eventually referred to a cooperative hospital at Perinthalmanna, in Malappuram district, a two-and-a-half-hour drive away from home. She died here, on April 13, 2026.
Rani and her husband Chandra Sekhar say the hospital refused to release their daughter’s body until they paid a bill of ₹10,000. They managed to raise the money with the help of a ward councillor.
“We buried her under that tree,” says Rani, pointing to a coconut tree near their house at Vechapathi hamlet in Sholayur panchayat of Attappadi, Palakkad district.

Dakshina’s death is among a series of 10 infant deaths reported this year from Attappadi, a predominantly tribal settlement. There have been four back-to-back deaths in October. Of the 10 infant deaths, six involved congenital anomalies, with heart defects among the commonly reported conditions. An expert committee of doctors and researchers is examining the deaths.

articles.title: U.S. blocks China’s remote access to AI chips after Nvidia scandal; China slams move
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Nvidia’s provision of chips to companies running data centres in Southeast Asia has come under the spotlight amid questions surrounding founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the CEO of one such Singapore-based company, Megaspeed

The United States has announced new regulations aimed at curbing Chinese firms’ remote access to advanced AI chips through data centres in third party countries, coming amid the scandal surrounding chipmaker Nvidia. Beijing on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) slammed the new restrictions, accusing Washington of “abusing export control measures”.

Nvidia’s provision of chips to companies running data centres in Southeast Asia has come under the spotlight amid questions surrounding founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang , the CEO of one such Singapore-based company, Megaspeed . With Nvidia barred from selling its most advanced chips in China, many Chinese companies instead sought access to its technology through data centres in countries such as Malaysia.

The U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced an interim final rule (IFR) “to address remote access” to advanced AI chips and servers, saying it was “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries.”

The new rule was announced days before President Donald Trump’s arrival in Shenzhen for meetings with President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the November 18-19 APEC Summit, which will also see a rare trilateral leaders’ summit along with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The rule states that in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required “to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil”, which it named as “countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.”

China hit out at the moves, calling it “yet another case of the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing export control measures to interfere in normal trade and tech cooperation between China and other countries and go after China’s high-tech industry.”

“Such typical economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction run counter to the common understandings between the two countries, harm the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies, and disrupt global supply chains,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said. “China will do what is necessary to firmly safeguard its legitimate and lawful rights and interests.”

China’s Ministry of Commerce in a statement said the new rule would affect the stability of the global semiconductor industry, adding that the U.S. was “misusing export controls to interfere indiscriminately in normal trade cooperation between Chinese enterprises and companies from other countries.” “The U.S. approach runs counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, undermines market rules and the international economic and trade order, and affects the stability of the global semiconductor industry and supply chain,” the statement said.

articles.title: West Bengal BJP president Samik Bhattacharya calls for protest over attacks on Hindus in Bangladesh
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: State BJP chief claims Bangladesh was created on the basis of religion, not language, as Bengali-speaking Hindus are now being persecuted and bearing the consequences of Partition
West Bengal Bharatiya Janata Party ( BJP ) president Samik Bhattacharya on Sunday (November 22, 2026) called for a protest against the alleged persecution of Hindus in Bangladesh .
“Blood is being shed in Bangladesh, and it is our brothers who are suffering. As a Bengali Hindu, I believe we must take to the streets,” the BJP leader told media persons.

Noting that India had played a crucial role in the creation of Bangladesh, the BJP Rajya Sabha MP expressed his opinion that Bangladesh was created on the basis of religion, not on the basis of the Bengali language.

“Bangladesh was not created for the sake of language. If it had been, Bengali-speaking Hindus in Bangladesh would not be dying like this today,” he said. Mr. Bhattacharya said that the fundamental question at that time should have been the protection of people and the creation of a democratic environment. Instead, the leadership surrendered to religious fundamentalism, he said.

Claiming that the wounds of Partition continued to haunt the subcontinent, the BJP leader said that it was religious minorities, particularly Hindus in Bangladesh, who were bearing the consequences. Blaming Partition on Jawaharlal Nehru and Mahatma Gandhi, Mr. Bhattacharya claimed that had Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose become independent India’s first Prime Minister, he would never have accepted the two-nation theory or allowed the subcontinent to be divided into India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.

The remarks by the West Bengal BJP leader come at a time when fresh political tensions have erupted in Bangladesh. Attempts at normalising the India-Bangladesh relationship in recent months have been hindered by former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s presence in India, where she took refuge on August 5, 2024. Ms. Hasina has announced that she is keen to return to Bangladesh.

fullParagraphs: Andhra Pradesh athletes secured three medals – one silver and two bronze – in the ongoing 1st India International Open Taekwondo Championship 2026, the tournament which is under way in Pune till November 25.

N. Sumitha, an 18-year-old athlete from Midhilesh Taekwondo Academy in Visakhapatnam, has bagged a bronze medal in the women’s Under-30 of poomsae category, while A. Nagaraju bagged a bronze medal in the men’s Under-50 individual poomsae event. Meanwhile, K. Surekha of Kurnool settled for a silver medal in the women’s Under-40 category.

Seven athletes trained by Mr. Pallam are taking part in the championship. A fourth-dan black belt, he is serving as a coach at the G1 international tournament. He has coached teams at the All India University, School Games Federation of India and CBSE levels, and is a national referee.

articles.title: Deepathoon row: Tamil Nadu files a review plea in Supreme Court against Thirupparankundram order
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The party urging a re-look of the court order must show that the findings were a result of a factual misconception or had ignored binding judicial precedents or violated a statutory mandate

Forty-eight hours before the lighting of the lamp at the deepathoon on Karthigai Deepam day on November 24, the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) department filed a review of the Supreme Court’s interim order allowing the “one-time limited arrangement”.

The HR&CE Commissioner argued that while the Supreme Court had stayed the Madras High Court’s January 6 direction to the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple Devasthanam to light the Karthigai Deepam on the Deepathoon located near a dargah on the summit of the hill, it had, in the same breath, allowed the lamp to be lit on the very same stone pillar on November 24, terming it a “limited one-time arrangement”, which would not be considered a precedent or a judicial recognition of a vested right.
The State’s review petition said this specific portion of the top court’s November 20 order was an “error apparent on the face of the record”.

articles.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties resume talks to form Israel government
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Likud laid down conditions for a unity government, including no Arab parties and rejection of a Palestinian state, while Gadi Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government

The parties of caretaker Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot launched a new round of talks on Sunday (November 22, 2026) over whether to form a coalition government, with Mr. Netanyahu’s party insisting on keeping his main policies.

Delegations from Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud began their meeting at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, an AFP journalist on the scene said, following a first round of talks on Sunday (November 15, 2026).

A former Chief of Staff of the army, Mr. Eisenkot has until December 6, 2026, to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after the October 2026 elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.

His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.
Mr. Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel.

Such an arrangement could allow him to keep his political protection against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.

But that prospect runs up against Mr. Eisenkot’s refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Mr. Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign. His ally, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, also reiterated on Saturday (November 21, 2026) his refusal to join a coalition with “Netanyahu or his bloc, under any circumstances”.

On Saturday (November 21, 2026), Yashar presented the resumption of talks as “a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government”, saying Mr. Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options. But Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, a formula backed by Mr. Netanyahu.

Among other things, it demands an end to “all personal attacks and incitement to hatred” targeting the outgoing Prime Minister and his government. It also called for bringing together “all the parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people”, without the participation of Arab parties. Mr. Netanyahu and his allies regularly target Arab parties, which secured a record 19 seats in the legislature and are opposed to his remaining in power.

Likud is also demanding agreement on several major policy positions, notably rejecting the creation of a Palestinian state, maintaining Israeli control over territories in Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, and a compromise on conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, a particularly sensitive issue in Israel.

articles.title: Ex-U.K. PM Theresa May tells successor to ‘move on’ from Brexit
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Former British Prime Minister Theresa May said she was “aghast” that Prime Minister Andy Burnham could be considering rejoining the European Union, after he sealed trade and youth mobility deals in Brussels

Ms. May’s remarks came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU’s top officials on Friday (November 20, 2026) sealed deals at a Brussels summit to ease trade and youth mobility. A decade after Britain narrowly voted to leave the bloc, Mr. Burnham has re-energised talk of closer ties ahead of a government 10-year plan for the U.K., set to be unveiled next month.

Ms. May warned that negotiations with the EU risked taking up vast amounts of government time, hampering efforts to tackle other issues. “And that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU,” she said.

Ms. May, who supported remaining in the 27-member bloc, said government had to respect the result of the 2016 referendum. “When I became prime minister, I was very clear. People have voted for Brexit. We should deliver Brexit,” she told BBC television.

“He (Burnham) wants to pat them (voters) on their head and say ‘you know what? Remember that vote? Well you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come up with the right answer’,” she said. Ms. May was forced to quit in May 2019 after failing to get her Brexit deal through parliament.

“My message to him (Burnham) really is: People voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on,” she added. Mr. Burnham, who has been in office since July 2026, has committed to his predecessor Keir Starmer’s “red lines” on Europe for this parliament, meaning no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement. But pro-Brexit campaigners fear he will push at some point to rejoin the 27-nation grouping.
Europe Minister Hamish Falconer said the world had changed since 2016, and the U.K. needed to “think over the long term about our relationship with Europe”.

“That’s why the prime minister is going to set out more next month as part of the 10-year plan about the long-term relationship between the UK and the EU,” he told Sky News . But he insisted the British people “are going to be the boss of every stage of this”.
“We are talking, as the prime minister was clear, about the long term. We will have a general election before then. People will be able to express their views,” he said.
Following Mr. Burnham’s EU deals, legislation to allow the U.K. to align with certain EU rules, including on food standards, is due to be introduced in parliament this week.

Former British Prime Minister Theresa May said she was “aghast” that Prime Minister Andy Burnham could be considering rejoining the European Union, after he sealed trade and youth mobility deals in Brussels

Ms. May’s remarks came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU’s top officials on Friday (November 20, 2026) sealed deals at a Brussels summit to ease trade and youth mobility. A decade after Britain narrowly voted to leave the bloc, Mr. Burnham has re-energised talk of closer ties ahead of a government 10-year plan for the U.K., set to be unveiled next month.

Ms. May warned that negotiations with the EU risked taking up vast amounts of government time, hampering efforts to tackle other issues. “And that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU,” she said.

Ms. May, who supported remaining in the 27-member bloc, said government had to respect the result of the 2016 referendum. “When I became prime minister, I was very clear. People have voted for Brexit. We should deliver Brexit,” she told BBC television.

“He (Burnham) wants to pat them (voters) on their head and say ‘you know what? Remember that vote? Well you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come up with the right answer’,” she said. Ms. May was forced to quit in May 2019 after failing to get her Brexit deal through parliament.

“My message to him (Burnham) really is: People voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on,” she added. Mr. Burnham, who has been in office since July 2026, has committed to his predecessor Keir Starmer’s “red lines” on Europe for this parliament, meaning no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement. But pro-Brexit campaigners fear he will push at some point to rejoin the 27-nation grouping.

Europe Minister Hamish Falconer said the world had changed since 2016, and the U.K. needed to “think over the long term about our relationship with Europe”.

“That’s why the prime minister is going to set out more next month as part of the 10-year plan about the long-term relationship between the UK and the EU,” he told Sky News . But he insisted the British people “are going to be the boss of every stage of this”.

“We are talking, as the prime minister was clear, about the long term. We will have a general election before then. People will be able to express their views,” he said.

Following Mr. Burnham’s EU deals, legislation to allow the U.K. to align with certain EU rules, including on food standards, is due to be introduced in parliament this week.

articles.title: Nvidia faces U.S. accounting probe amid deepening turmoil: media
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Securities and Exchange Commission inquiry is in its early stages, U.S. media reported, after Jensen Huang’s resignation as chief executive and a 14% fall in Nvidia shares on Friday (November 20, 2026)

U.S. securities regulators are investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia, according to U.S. media, adding to the turmoil engulfing the artificial intelligence chip giant following the resignation of its chief executive.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry is in its early stages, The New York Times reported on Saturday (November 21, 2026), citing people briefed on the confidential investigation. The Wall Street Journal reported on the investigation earlier this week, although it was unable to establish its precise focus. The probe could end without any charges being brought against the company.

Questions about Nvidia’s financial disclosures have intensified amid scrutiny of its dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company investigated by American authorities over suspected shipments of restricted AI chips to China. Nvidia last year changed how it reported sales by geographical location, switching from customers’ billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered, U.S. media reported.

The change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown, despite the company’s significant business there. It remains unclear whether the SEC investigation is connected to those accounting changes or to the scandal surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang.

Mr. Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of working for Beijing. China has denied the espionage allegations, while Megaspeed has maintained that it operates lawfully.
Nvidia’s board has appointed former chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive, and launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding Mr. Huang’s departure.

The upheaval has shaken investor confidence in one of the world’s most valuable companies, whose advanced semiconductors have been central to the global AI boom. Nvidia shares plunged 14% on Friday (November 20, 2026), bringing their losses for the week to more than 20%.

U.S. President Donald Trump nevertheless called on Friday (November 20, 2026) for Mr. Huang to be reinstated. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Mr. Trump told reporters. But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones has ruled out his return, saying board directors unanimously accepted his resignation.

articles.title: Iran strike wounds two in Bahrain, Riyadh denounces ‘criminal’ attacks
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Bahrain said two people were wounded in an attack on “a civilian industrial site”, while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they targeted U.S. air defence systems.

Bahrain on Sunday (November 22, 2026) said two people were wounded in an Iranian attack on Saturday (November 21, 2026) against “a civilian industrial site” in the kingdom, which has repeatedly come under attack in recent days.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have repeatedly said they targeted U.S. facilities in Bahrain, where Iranian strikes resumed on November 13 after a lull since early September.
“In the wake of the criminal Iranian attacks suffered yesterday (Saturday) by the Kingdom of Bahrain... a Bahraini national with a disability was wounded,” Bahrain’s Interior Ministry said on X.
“His condition is stable. A Pakistani resident was also wounded and is in critical condition. Both are being treated in hospital.”
Two residents told AFP they had seen smoke rising above Sitra Island, east of Manama, which hosts several industrial facilities, including a refinery operated by the state-owned oil company Bapco.

In a statement carried by Iranian state media on Saturday evening, the Revolutionary Guards said they had attacked with missiles and drones U.S. Patriot air defence systems at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, in response to the “continued violations of the airspace” of the Islamic Republic.
Tehran said on Saturday it had intercepted a U.S. drone targeting Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic maritime corridor at the heart of the war in West Asia.

Bahrain’s powerful neighbour Saudi Arabia on Sunday lambasted Tehran for its continued “brutal aggression” against Gulf countries. In a statement published on X, the Saudi Foreign Ministry expressed “the strongest condemnation and denunciation by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia of the criminal Iranian attacks against a civilian industrial facility in the brotherly Kingdom of Bahrain”.

Saudi Arabia also announced early on Sunday that it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis in the west of the kingdom. The region is home to key energy infrastructure, including the oil terminal at the port of Yanbu, as well as the Jizan refinery, located in the far southwest of the country, near the border with Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighbouring Yemen’s civil war this summer, the latest front in the West Asia war.
